Psychology as Science. The late-nineteenth-century transition of psychology from philosophical speculation to controlled laboratory experimentation.

Wilhelm Wundt opened the first experimental psychology laboratory in Leipzig in eighteen seventy-nine, establishing psychology as a formal academic discipline distinct from philosophy. This marked the professionalization of psychological inquiry. Wundt's method of introspection involved carefully trained observers reporting on their own mental experiences under controlled conditions, aiming to make consciousness scientifically observable, paralleling physics and chemistry's instrumentation.

William James developed American experimental psychology by embracing functionalism, asking how consciousness and behavior serve adaptive purposes rather than just describing mental structures. James emphasized the stream of consciousness. Early experimental psychologists studied reaction time through mental chronometry, visual perception, memory, attention, and association using instruments like tachistoscopes and chronographs, establishing empirical method through quantitative measurement.

The scientific establishment of psychology created debate: could consciousness truly be measured objectively using third-person methods, or would quantification necessarily exclude important subjective phenomena only accessible through introspection? G. Stanley Hall and James McKeen Cattell brought experimental psychology into educational and applied settings, establishing the field's practical relevance beyond the laboratory.

This period established psychology's twin aspirations: rigor through controlled experimentation, quantification, and reproducibility, and relevance in addressing practical human concerns in education, work, and clinical settings. The emergence of scientific psychology fundamentally challenged philosophy's monopoly on mind, establishing psychology as an empirical science investigating the mechanisms of consciousness and behavior through experimentation.
